hits.text:
Opus 5.5 now runs twice on the same Blender build, and the second copy is paid to prove the first one wrong

Running one model twice as long does not make it more careful. Running two in parallel, with opposite jobs, does.

> BUILD - one instance produces geometry, hierarchy and materials end to end
> CHALLENGE - the other works the same brief looking only for where that build breaks
> MERGE - conflicts resolved against the brief, never by whichever model argued louder

Sequential review wastes the clock. The checker sits idle while the builder works, then the builder sits idle during review.

In parallel both finish together. The wait collapses to a single pass instead of two stacked on top of each other.

The challenger never sees itself as a builder. It has no draft to defend, so it has no reason to approve anything.

Resolving against the brief is what keeps it honest. The original request is the referee, not either model’s confidence.

Quality goes up for the same reason code review works: nobody catches their own blind spot by staring harder.

The brief, both outputs and the full conflict log are laid out underneath.

i copied my whole brain into Grok Bot, handed it $40,000 a month of clients and gave it one rule: "lose one and i delete you". then i flew to bali for 30 days

a second brain is one folder that knows everything i know: every client, every price, every promise, the way i write. Grok Bot reads it before every task, on its own computer in the cloud, laptop shut

one evening, no code:

> me.md: my work, my clients, what i owe each of them
> voice.md: how i write, pulled from my last 100 emails
> people/: one page per client, every promise linked to the email it came from
> rules.md: every mistake i catch, it reads before every task

then i left

→ day 1: it filed 212 client emails into the right pages while i was on the plane
→ day 3: it quoted a client last year's price from memory. i caught it, one line went into rules.md, it hasn't happened since
→ day 9: a client asked "what did we agree in march?" it pulled the exact email in 40 seconds
→ day 21: it flagged a deadline 2 days too late. that client left
→ day 30: it also signed 2 new ones, so it stays

honestly the best part is one question i ask it every monday: "what are 5 things you could do for me this week?" that's how it found the 2 new clients: past clients who'd asked for more work and never heard back

by week 4 it was writing replies i couldn't tell from mine

someone's second brain is already answering your clients faster than you

hits.text:
Anthropic engineering team stopped letting models touch the app and gave them a script layer instead, and the whole thing got faster overnight

A model holding the tool directly has to understand the tool. A model writing a script only has to understand the job.

> READ - the task parsed once into what has to change, never into UI steps
> WRITE - the model emits a script instead of clicking through an interface
> RUN - the script executes natively, at the speed the software actually works
> CHECK - the result verified against the task, not against what the model intended
> KEEP - scripts that worked saved, so the same job never gets re-reasoned

Direct tool use looks impressive and runs slowly. Every action is a round trip: look, decide, act, look again.

A script collapses all of that into one pass. The thinking happens once, the execution happens at machine speed.

The keep step is where it compounds. The second time a job appears, there is nothing to generate at all.

Verification against the task matters more than it sounds. A script that runs cleanly can still do the wrong thing confidently.

Most agent stacks are slow for this exact reason. Not weak models, just models forced to operate software one click at a time.

The script layer, the verification rules and a full before-and-after run are laid out underneath.
